title: A Trusted Contact Isn’t a Co-Owner
subtitle: When someone you love needs help with money, the title on an account or form matters. A trusted contact, a power-of-attorney agent and a joint owner have different roles—and different consequences.
imageAlt: Two adult siblings and an older relative sit at a kitchen table, reviewing a folder of financial papers together.
imageConcept: A specific, natural kitchen-table scene: two adult siblings and an older relative compare account paperwork in a calm conversation, with a closed laptop and ordinary household details nearby; no visible account numbers or staged distress.
body: Start with the question behind the paperwork

A family member is missing bills, struggling to keep track of statements or planning for a future health change. Someone offers to help. That sounds straightforward until a form asks whether the helper should be a trusted contact, an agent under a power of attorney or a joint account owner. Those are not interchangeable labels. Each creates a different relationship to the account holder’s money and decisions.

The useful first question is not simply, “Who do we trust?” It is, “What kind of help is needed, and what authority would that require?” Perhaps the person wants company while sorting mail. Perhaps they want someone to speak with a brokerage firm if the firm cannot reach them. Perhaps they want another person to pay bills if they can no longer manage them. The right arrangement depends on that distinction, the account terms and, in the United States, state law. This is general financial education, not a recommendation about which arrangement any particular family should choose.
A trusted contact is a point of contact, not a substitute decision-maker

A trusted contact listed with a brokerage firm can give the firm someone to contact in certain circumstances. The designation does not, by itself, let that person decide what to buy or sell, withdraw funds or execute transactions. FINRA’s January 2026 notice reiterates that a trusted contact has no authority to make decisions about the customer’s brokerage account or carry out transactions [1].

That boundary can be reassuring: adding a trusted contact is not the same as handing over control. It can also prevent a painful misunderstanding. A relative may assume that being named on a form means they can step in; the account holder may believe the firm will call that person to pay an urgent bill. Neither assumption follows from the designation alone.

The scope matters, too. FINRA’s trusted-contact rules concern brokerage-firm accounts, not every bank, retirement or household account. Ask the specific institution what the designation allows it to do, when it might reach out and what information it may share. A trusted contact can help with communication; other tools are needed when someone is meant to act.
Help can begin without handing over account access

Many useful forms of support do not require changing ownership or granting transaction authority. Someone can sit with a relative while they sort statements, make a list of due dates, compare a bill with a bank transaction or help prepare questions for a financial institution. The account holder can remain the person who signs, approves and makes payments. A family can agree on a narrow task, such as reviewing bills together once a month, and revisit it if needs change.

That approach is not always enough. If the account holder wants another person to make payments or speak with an institution as an authorized representative, the institution may require a formal arrangement. The CFPB lists convenience bank accounts as one possible arrangement for helping with banking and says safeguards should be used to prevent misuse of the money [3]. Before agreeing to any setup, ask the bank or credit union what the helper can do, and what records or permissions are required. The CFPB says that hiring someone to help with financial services generally does not require adding that person to a bank account, and lists convenience accounts, carefully written powers of attorney and trusts as possible ways to arrange help, with safeguards against misuse [3].
A power of attorney grants authority under a document

A power of attorney, or POA, is a legal document that allows another person to act on someone’s behalf. A financial POA may be prepared in advance so the named agent can help manage financial matters if needed. The CFPB says a family member or friend may name a fiduciary through a POA to help manage money or property if they are unable to do so; an accepted fiduciary must follow the POA’s instructions and terms [2].

The CFPB says a POA can name a fiduciary to help manage another person’s money or property, and that the fiduciary must follow the POA’s instructions and terms [2]. The account holder should understand when the authority begins, which tasks it covers and how it can be revoked, where applicable.

 Ask the institution what it needs before an urgent moment, and consult a qualified legal professional about state-specific requirements.
Joint ownership changes more than access

Adding someone as a joint owner can give that person substantial access, including the ability to withdraw money while both owners are alive. That is a different arrangement from authorizing someone to help with bills or naming them as a trusted contact. The CFPB notes that hiring someone to help with financial services generally does not require making that person a joint account owner [3].

Ownership after one account holder dies is another important distinction: the CFPB says joint bank accounts usually let the surviving owner retain the money in the account [3]. A family should not assume that the balance will automatically go to the person who contributed most, paid the bills or was added most recently. Ask the bank or credit union to explain the account’s ownership terms in writing, and consider how the change could affect other plans.

Before signing, make the trade-off concrete: Could the added owner withdraw the full balance? What happens if one owner dies? Could the arrangement complicate the account holder’s plans or create conflict among relatives? Those are not reasons every joint account is wrong; they are reasons to understand what is being granted.
Authority is a responsibility, not a benefit

When an agent acts under a POA, the role is not permission to treat another person’s funds as their own. A fiduciary must act for the other person’s benefit, manage money carefully, keep it separate and maintain good records, according to the CFPB [2]. In practical terms, that means the agent should be able to explain what each payment was for and show where the money went.

Clear records protect both people. Keep receipts, account statements and a simple log of transactions made for the account holder. Avoid mixing the person’s money with the agent’s own funds. If the agent is paying a bill on someone else’s behalf, record the date, amount, recipient and purpose. These habits make it easier to answer questions later and reduce the chance that ordinary family support is mistaken for an unexplained transfer.

A fiduciary role can carry serious duties, and the document and law define the agent’s authority. Someone asked to serve should understand the job before accepting it. Someone choosing an agent can ask how that person will keep records, handle conflicts and communicate about decisions.
Prepare before there is a deadline

A calm conversation can start with a specific task rather than a broad discussion of aging or incapacity. “Would it help if I sat with you while you sort the utility bills?” is more concrete than “I should take over your finances.” If the answer is yes, agree on what the helper may see or do, what remains private and when you will check whether the arrangement still works.

For any formal step, write down the questions to take to the institution or an appropriate professional. What does this form authorize? Can the person make withdrawals or only receive information? Does authority apply immediately or only under stated conditions? What happens if the account holder changes their mind? Does the institution have its own process, and what does state law require? With a POA, ask how the bank will review it; with a joint account, ask about access and ownership after death; with a trusted contact, ask when the firm may call.

Keep the account holder involved for as long as they want and are able to participate. A helper’s convenience is not a reason to grant broader authority than necessary. Nor should a person be pressured to sign a document or change an account on the spot.
Make the conversation about the help—not the label

Try this sequence: name the difficulty, ask what support would feel useful, and identify the smallest step that addresses it. Then separate communication from decision-making and decision-making from ownership. If a formal authority may be needed, pause long enough to understand the document, the institution’s requirements and the state-specific rules before proceeding.

The goal is not to find one perfect form for every family. It is to make sure everyone understands what a choice does—and does not—allow. A trusted contact can be useful without being a co-owner. A POA can give an agent authority without making that person the owner. A joint account can provide access while also changing the ownership relationship. Naming the distinction clearly is a practical act of care: it protects the account holder’s control while making room for help that is genuinely wanted.
